cards.a: Shaping smooths traffic to a rate by buffering excess instead of dropping it. It works egress-only and adds delay, making it ideal for aligning to a subscribed line rate or a downstream policer without wasting packets.

cards.q: How does shaping handle excess traffic compared to policing?
cards.a: Shaping buffers the excess in a shaping queue and it goes out later, adding delay; policing drops or re-marks excess with no delay. Shaping is egress-only with low loss; policing works ingress/egress with high loss.

cards.q: What are the elements of the shaping model?
cards.a: CIR (the shaped rate), Bc (committed burst), Be (excess burst), the queue that buffers excess, and added delay/latency.

cards.q: Why would you use shaping rather than policing?
cards.a: To align to the access line CIR, avoid drops by not exceeding a downstream policer, smooth bursts for fairness, and avoid flooding a downstream link. Shaping protects against bursty transmission hitting a stricter link.

cards.q: What command configures shaping and how do 'shape average' and 'shape peak' differ?
cards.a: shape average <rate> uses a token bucket (Bc/Be) and is the standard; shape peak permits use of Be to allow extra burst. It is configured in a policy-map attached with service-policy output.
A parent policy shapes the aggregate/total rate (e.g., 10 Mbps) while child policies carve per-class sub-rates, resulting in per-class buckets within the link rate.

cards.q: What command shows shaping statistics on an interface?
cards.a: show policy-map interface (or show policy-map interface Gi0/1), along with show queueing interface.

cards.q: A shaper is adding excessive delay; what is the likely cause and what should you check?
cards.a: Queue buildup in the shaper's queue. Check the queueing depth/buffer, and ensure the shaped rate matches the link.

cards.q: Traffic bursts are leaking through a shaper; what is the likely cause?
cards.a: The Bc/Be burst values are too small. Increase Bc so legitimate bursts are buffered and released at the shaped rate.

cards.q: What is the fundamental difference between shaping and policing?
cards.a: Shaping buffers excess and adds delay; policing drops or re-marks the excess with no buffering.

cards.q: On what direction(s) does shaping apply?
cards.a: Shaping is egress-only; policing can be applied on ingress or egress.

cards.q: For smoothing traffic to an access line rate, should you shape or police?
cards.a: Shape, because shaping buffers and smooths bursts to align with the CIR without dropping, whereas policing would drop the excess.
